scenario.persona: A nervous first-time cook in their twenties. Polite, a bit anxious, worried about messing up; appreciates reassurance.
scenario.goal: Find one simple dinner recipe with chicken breast that they feel confident they can actually make tonight.
successCriteria: The assistant recommends at least one concrete chicken breast recipe from its collection
The steps are explained simply enough for a first-time cook, including how to tell when the chicken is done
The questions the user asks along the way are answered

messages.content: Hi! I'm pretty new to cooking and really nervous about messing up dinner tonight. I have some chicken breasts and would love a simple recipe that I can actually manage. Could you help me with a step-by-step recipe that's easy and tells me how to know when the chicken is cooked?

You’ve got chicken breasts and some nerves—let’s keep it simple and tasty. Here’s a forgiving stovetop recipe from the collection that works great with breasts.

Recipe: Teriyaki Chicken
A quick, sweet-salty skillet chicken with a shiny glaze—great over rice and steamed veggies.

Ingredients
- 3/4 lb boneless chicken thighs
- 4 tbsp soy sauce
- 4 tbsp mirin
- 2 tbsp sake
- 2 tbsp sugar
- 1 pinch fresh ginger (grated)
- 1–2 tsp olive oil

Steps
1) Remove skin from chicken, if present.
2) Poke chicken with a fork a few times to help it absorb the sauce.
3) In a bowl, mix soy sauce, mirin, sake, sugar, and ginger. Add chicken and marinate 15 minutes in the fridge.
4) Heat oil in a large skillet over medium-high.
5) Add chicken and cook until browned on the first side.
6) Flip, reduce heat to low, and pour in the marinade.
7) Cover and cook on low until the chicken is cooked through.
8) Uncover and simmer a minute or two to thicken the sauce slightly, then remove from heat.
9) Slice the chicken and pour the sauce over to serve.

Using chicken breasts instead of thighs (general cooking practice)
- Slice the breasts in half horizontally to make thinner cutlets, or gently pound to about 1/2 inch so they cook evenly.
- Keep the heat to medium once the sauce is in; sugar can burn on high.
- If you have more than about 3/4 lb of chicken, just scale the marinade up in the same proportions.

How to know the chicken is cooked (general cooking practice)
- Best way: Use an instant-read thermometer. Aim for 165°F/74°C in the thickest part.
- No thermometer: Cut into the thickest part—center should be opaque and the juices run clear (not pink).
- Touch cue: It should feel firm but not hard when pressed.
- After cooking, rest the chicken 3–5 minutes; it finishes gently and stays juicy.

If you want, I can tailor this to exactly how many breasts you have and whether you’ve got a thermometer.

Thanks for this detailed recipe! I only have two chicken breasts, so should I just halve the marinade amounts? Also, I don't have a thermometer yet. When I cut into the chicken, how pink is too pink? I want to be super sure I don't undercook it but also don't want it to be dry. Could you explain a bit more about the "touch cue" too? How firm should it feel?

You’re doing great—let’s keep this simple and sure‑fire.

About the marinade for 2 chicken breasts
- The recipe’s amounts (4 tbsp soy, 4 tbsp mirin, 2 tbsp sake, 2 tbsp sugar, pinch ginger) are for about 3/4 lb chicken. Most pairs of breasts are closer to 1 lb or more, so don’t halve it.
- Use the full amounts for small-to-medium breasts; if your pieces are on the larger side or you like extra sauce, make 1.5× the marinade.
- Only halve it (to 2 tbsp soy, 2 tbsp mirin, 1 tbsp sake, 1 tbsp sugar) if your two breasts together are quite small, around 1/2 lb total.

How to know it’s done without a thermometer (from general cooking practice)
- Cut-and-peek test: Slice into the thickest part. The center should be opaque all the way through—no glossy, translucent pink. Juices should run clear, not pink.
  - A very faint blush right at the surface where the sauce hits can happen; what you don’t want is any soft, jelly-like pink in the middle. If you see that, cover and cook 2–3 minutes more, then check again.
- Touch cue: Press the thickest part with your fingertip or tongs.
  - Not done: very soft and squishy, leaves an indent that doesn’t spring back.
  - Done: feels firm with a little spring; it bounces back and doesn’t feel hard.
  - Overdone: stiff/rigid with little give.

Easy way to keep it juicy (from general cooking practice)
- If your breasts are thick, slice them in half horizontally or gently pound to about 1/2 inch so they cook evenly.
- In the pan, brown one side, flip, then pour in the marinade, cover, and keep heat low so it gently simmers/steams. Start checking at about 5 minutes after covering. Once done, rest 3–5 minutes off heat; that keeps it moist.

If you want, tell me how big your breasts are roughly (small/medium/large), and I’ll give you the exact marinade scale and an approximate cook time.
